abstract: Terrain-aware locomotion training requires both fast simulation and enough temporal experience for policy learning. We combine Isaac Gym simulation and proximal policy optimization on a single GPU, reducing data transfers while collecting experience from thousands of robots. An adaptive curriculum moves robots between tiled terrains according to traversal performance, progressively exposing them to harder terrain without regenerating meshes. The policy uses proprioception and local terrain heights; training incorporates friction randomization, observation noise, pushes, and actuator modeling for transfer. PPO adaptations include large minibatches and time-out bootstrapping, while adequate per-robot rollout lengths constrain usable parallelism. On an NVIDIA RTX A6000 workstation, training with 4,096 robots, 98,304 samples per batch, and 1,500 updates took under 20 minutes. Simulated stair crossings without base contact achieved nearly 100% success for steps up to 0.2 m, but obstacle success declined with difficulty and uphill traversal failed beyond 25 degrees. The fixed policy negotiated stairs and obstacles on physical ANYmal C, although imperfect lidar-derived terrain maps reduced robustness and required limiting velocity commands to 0.6 m/s. These experiments support rapid training and hardware deployment under this setup, with limits imposed by rollout duration, terrain difficulty, and mapping quality.
methods: PPO's critic estimates discounted return beyond the current rollout, so reset handling must reflect why a trajectory stops. Failure or goal completion is a task termination that the critic can predict. A time limit instead interrupts an otherwise continuing task: episode time is excluded from observations, leaving the critic unable to anticipate that reset. Treating it as terminal would discard the expected future return and distort the value target. The implementation therefore exposes time-outs separately through a modified environment interface. At a time-out, the reward is augmented by the critic's discounted prediction of remaining return, so its training target retains a continuation value instead of treating the reset as an ordinary terminal transition. This distinction matters because episodes last up to 20 seconds and span multiple short data-collection batches. Resets need not coincide with batch boundaries, and finishing a PPO batch does not itself reset an environment.
results: Figure 4 identifies an intermediate reward-time trade-off, not a monotonic benefit from adding robots. The comparison uses a simplified task with reduced maximum stair and obstacle heights and no curriculum; reward is summarized as mean and standard deviation over five runs after 1,500 policy updates. At fixed batch size, adding robots shortens each robot's rollout and reduces training time, but excessive parallelism sharply lowers reward. This is consistent with insufficient temporal context for advantage estimation. Throughput gains also slow beyond roughly 4,000 robots. At the other extreme, fewer robots yield somewhat lower reward; reduced sample diversity from longer, correlated trajectories is the authors' proposed explanation. Larger batches improve reward and postpone the high-parallelism decline, but take longer to train. The million-sample baseline with 20,000 robots gives the highest reward at greater training cost. For this task, about 2,048-4,096 robots with roughly 100,000-200,000 samples per batch offer the preferred balance. This operating range reflects both temporal-data requirements and throughput saturation, rather than an argument for unlimited parallelism.
notes: Figure 4's exact reward values, training times, and standard deviations are unavailable in the declared text; only reported trends are interpreted. Hardware demonstrations are not assigned a success rate. The selected 98,304-sample batch with 4,096 robots implies 24 rollout steps; the reported difficulty below 25 steps is not treated as a universal cutoff. Additional robot policies were retrained, with changes needed for A1 and Cassie. Proposed teacher-student integration remains future work.
